problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1).$

activity_context.topic_title: The Gradient as a Normal Vector

examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Surface
examples.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z) = 2x^2 - xy - z^2,$ find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2).$
examples.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2)$ can be found by computing 
$\nabla f(2, 3, \sqrt 2).$   

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }k \\  & =(4x-y)\text{ }i-x\text{ }j-2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,3,\sqrt{2}) & =(4\cdot 2-3)\text{ }i-2\text{ }j-2\sqrt{2}\text{ }k \\  & =5i-2j-2\sqrt{2}\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $5 \mathbf i  - 2 \mathbf j - 2 \sqrt 2\ \mathbf k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2).$

feedback.problem: Consider the plane curve $\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+{y}^{2}=1.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(3,0).$
feedback.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(3,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =\frac{2}{9}x\,i+2y\,j \\ ∇f(3,0) & =\frac{2}{9}(3)\,i+2(0)\,j \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\,i \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{3},0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,0)=⟨\frac{2}{3},0⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-{x}_{0}){v}_{y}-(y-{y}_{0}){v}_{x} & =0 \\ (x-3)0-(y-0)\frac{2}{3} & =0 \\ -\frac{2}{3}y & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$
